The evidence supports this in two ways: 1) It explicitly states that 'surface-related TAA techniques, such as using the geometry and depth buffer to detect disocclusions, are not viable' for froxel data because it describes in-scattering at a point in space rather than on a surface. 2) It confirms that reprojection is done 'using a reprojection vector that describes how the camera was moved and rotated,' and that this vector 'only contains information about how the camera moved.' Thus, the evidence confirms that geometric disocclusion handling (via depth/geometry buffers) is not part of the process, and only camera motion is used.

Ideal for real-time volumetric fog and lighting where performance is critical and single-sample rendering is too aliased [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the technique is ideal for real-time volumetric fog and lighting where performance is critical and single-sample rendering is too aliased. The evidence explicitly supports this in Section 2.3, stating: 'The computationally heavy nature of evaluating participating media necessitates one sample per froxel per frame, which on its own results in a heavily aliased output. By re-using froxel data from the previous frame and blending it with new samples, it is possible to achieve an effectively supersampled volume at very little extra performance cost. This is known as temporal accumulation and is a key tool in modern real-time volumetric rendering.' This directly confirms that single-sample rendering is aliased, performance is a critical factor (hence the need for 'very little extra performance cost'), and the technique is used for real-time volumetric lighting.

It confirms that the resulting blended radiance is stored in a history buffer for the next frame. Since the system processes N froxels per frame and maintains a history buffer of the same size (plus the current frame grid), the memory complexity is linear with respect to the number of froxels, O(N).
